item.title: Docker
item.description:
docker is an app that makes migrating systems, servers, databases, etc. a lot easier. the way docker does it is with Images and Containers. just let the next machine install docker only, and it's ready to migrate!if you don't use docker when migrating. the system might break it could be because of outdated / unstable software, no prerequisite packages. inconsistent configuration. and more.
Images are one of the key features of Docker. Images are packages that are ready to be copied and deployed to your Container so it can be used immediately.
Analogy think of an Image as a photo of a document. you can still read the document right? but you can't edit it, just scan it.
once the Image has been scanned. it can then be edited again and be used again
Containers are also one of the key features of Docker. Containers are basically tiny virtual machines with their own apps and services running. and those services would be your running Images. mysql php docker network create [[name of network]] Example docker network create webdev-network DISCLAIMER NOT RECOMMENDED TO RUN THIS BY ITSELF docker run --d [[name of container]] netstat -ano | findstr [portnumber] Example netstat -anp | findstr 3306 if something is using port 3306, otherwise, it would just do nothing. TCP 0.0.0.0:3306 0.0.0.0:0 LISTENING 18196 TCP [::]:3306 [::]:0 LISTENING 18196
in this part is where Containers are created the commands at the very bottom on this section are the commands you can use for our class and just rename them to what you want to makedocker run -d --name [ContainerName] --netwok [NetworkName] -v [Volume Name]:[Volume Location] -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=[Mysql Password] -e MYSQL_DATABASE=[DatabaseName] -p [container port]:[program port] [image to be installed] Example docker run -d --name webdev-mysql --network webdev-network -v webdev-dv-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=webdev-db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 docker run -d --name [ContainerName] --network [NetworkName] -e PMA_HOST=[MysqlContainerName] -p [container port]:[program port] [image to be installed] Example docker run -d --name webdev-phpmyadmin --network webdev-network -e PMA_HOST=webdev-mysql -p 3311:80 phpmyadmin DISCLAIMER DO NOT COPY THIS. THIS COMMAND IS IRRELEVANT TO YOUR PROJECTS docker run -d --name EB_mysql --network EB_Network -v EB-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=EB_shop -p 6967:3306 mysql:8.0 docker run -d --name EB_phpmyadmin --network EB_Network -e PMA_HOST=EB_mysql -p 6969:80 phpmyadmin From the notes of Sir Ariel Bensingdocker build -t symfony-app docker run --name symfony-app-demo --network platform-network -p 8000:8000 symfony-app docker network create platform-network docker run -d --name symfony-db --network platform-network -v symfony-db-data:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -e MYSQL_DATABASE=app_db -p 3310:3306 mysql:8.0 docker run -d --name symfony-pma --network platform-network -p 8081:80 -e PMA_HOST=symfony-db phpmyadmin docker exec -it symfony-app-demo “symfony command” docker network rm platform-network docker rm “container name” docker rmi “image name” docker network “network name” docker network rm “network name” docker stop “container name” on symfony to connect to your database you have to open your .env file on the root rolder.MYSQL_USER= MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP= MYSQL_PORT= MYSQL_DATABASE= Example My database has these variables to connect to. it doesn't mean you can copy this and make it work on yours. you have to provide your own values MYSQL_USER=root MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_IP=127.0.0.1 MYSQL_PORT=3306 MYSQL_DATABASE=eb_shop
on Making Variables we'll use the created variables there to connect to the database.DATABASE_URL="mysql://${MYSQL_USER}:${MYSQL_PASSWORD}@${MYSQL_IP}:${MYSQL_PORT}/${MYSQL_DATABASE}?serverVersion=10.11.2-MariaDB&charset=utf8mb4" you can copy this if you want

item.description:
Prerequisite Needs PHP 8.3 and above Need Internetsymfony new [Project Name] --webapp symfony server:start if you want to start the server on all available ip addresses on your network. add --allow-all-ipsymfony console make:controller [Controller Name] symfony console make:controller HomeController Example Scenario dev wants to make a "DashboardController". dev runs this command symfony console make:controller DashboardController this will create a file on /src/Controller/ and a folder with a file in /templates/ to access the controller. it has defaulted to 127.0.0.1:800x/dashboard and this is located on /src/Controller/DashboardController.php on line 11 looks like #[Route('/dashboard', name: 'app_dashboard')] <?php namespace App\Controller; use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController; use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response; use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route; final class DashboardController extends AbstractController { //this one right here #[Route('/dashboard', name: 'app_dashboard')] //this one right here public function index(): Response { return $this->render('dashboard/index.html.twig', [ 'controller_name' => 'DashboardController', ]); } } previously on Create new controller there was a mentioned /templates/dashboard. this is where you edit your HTML or PHP.in your file you will see these lines {% block body %} {% endblock %}. i don't know what these are called yet but they are used by the base.html.twig that we're gonna show later. inside that block is the HTML that is used for the body and if you look at /templates/base.html.twig you will see this <body> {% block body %}{% endblock %} </body> this is where the inside of your controller's {% block body %} {% endblock %} will appear in the actual websiteExample Scenario you want to add a simple hello world to the DashboardController simply go to /templates/dashboard/index.html.twig and replace what's inside the {% block body %}{% endblock %} with what you want in this case it will be {% block body %} <h1>Hello World</h1> {% endblock %} you don't have to edit base.html.twig because that's for reusable elements like the top navigation bar or the side bar, or even the footer.if you have elements like the top navigation bar, the Side Bar or the footer. you don't have to copy and paste the elements to other files over and over again.instead what you can do is change what is written in /templates/base.html.twig what happens here is base.html.twig loads first, then adds the {% block %}s afterin our discussion our teacher gave us an exampleExample Scenario dev wants the reusable part to be just the side bar and the contents be in another location. the side bar would be one with the <aside> tag <body> <div class="layout"> <aside class="sidebar"> <div class="sidebar-header"> <h2>My App</h2> </div> <nav> <ul> <li> <a href="{{ path('app_dashboard') }}">Dashboard</a> </li> <li> <a>Users</a> </li> <li> <a>Settings</a> </li> </ul> </nav> </aside> <main class="content"> {% block body %}{% endblock %} </main> </div> </body> by changing what's inside the <body> in the base.html.twig we have essentially created a reusable element.though this kinda looks intimidating. but when we use partial templates later. this script will look less intimidating.Partial templates are templates that don't have controllers. there are basically small components you can add to an exsisting .twig file.
in the previous example on How to Reuse Elements, the side bar took too much space on the body. let's change that by making Partial TemplatesExample Scenario dev wants previous code to look more cleaner. dev creates a folder named partials on /templates/ in /templates/partials/, dev creates a file to store the side bar. which will be named sidebar.html.twig inside /templates/partials/sidebar.html/twig dev will write the following <aside class="sidebar"> <div class="sidebar-header"> <h2>My App</h2> </div> <nav> <ul> <li> <a href="{{ path('app_dashboard') }}">Dashboard</a> </li> <li> <a>Users</a> </li> <li> <a>Settings</a> </li> </ul> </nav> </aside> since the file has been created. in /templates/base.html.twig replace what was written in the body with {% include '[path to partials]' %}, in our case, it will be {% include 'partials/sidebar.html.twig' %} /templates/base.html.twig will look something like this <body> <div class="layout"> {% include 'partials/sidebar.html.twig' %} <main class="content"> {% block body %}{% endblock %} </main> </div> </body> this way your code is separated and looks cleaner than before

item.title: finals
item.description: Form a group of 3-5 members Estrera Academia Orcullo Tejeros Leon system name Lavhanan Laundry Hub. The name of our project is the "Lavhanan Laundry Hub (Laundry hub management system)." We chose this name simply because it is the original name given by the business owner. Our main goal is to support the owner and help their business grow by bringing it online. We are not trying to change their shop, but rather extend it with new digital tools. By adding this online computer system, we want to make their daily work easier, keep their records more organized, and give their customers a better and faster way to track their laundry. Problem to be solved The Lavhanan laundry business has a few main problems that the new computer system needs to solve. First, the staff writes all the customer orders by hand in a logbook and uses small paper receipts, which makes it hard to keep detailed records. Second, because they do not usually count every piece of clothing, some customers try to claim that their items are missing or lost. Third, when people do not pay or forget to pick up their laundry, the workers have to manually search for the customer's phone number on paper and call them one by one. Fourth, adding up the daily sales is done by hand, which can be slow and difficult to manage. Finally, customers do not have a way to know exactly when their clothes are ready for pickup. The new system will fix these problems by saving all the information online, tracking exact item counts, calculating the daily money automatically, and sending automatic text messages directly to the customers. Target users The target users for the Lavhanan Laundry Hub are divided into two main groups: Employees and Customers. Here is a simple breakdown of how each role will use the system: Lavhanan Employees (Admin and Staff) Owner / Admin: Has full control over the computer system. They can see all the daily money earned, read the monthly sales reports, and manage the accounts for all other workers. Manager: Helps the owner watch over the daily business. They can look at all the laundry orders, make sure the work is not slow, and fix any big problems with the customers. Cashier: Welcomes the customer and takes the dirty laundry. They type the customer's name into the system, weigh the clothes, give the receipt, and mark the order as "paid" or "unpaid." Labandera (Laundry Worker): Does the physical washing. They use the system to simply update the steps of the laundry (clicking buttons to show if the clothes are washing, drying, folding, or ready). Delivery Driver: Uses the system to see the customer's home address and updates the app when the clean clothes are dropped off. (Even if the shop only does pickups right now, this prepares the system for the future). Lavhanan Customers People who bring their clothes to the shop. They use the simple online web app on their phones to check if their laundry is ready, see how much they need to pay, and ask the shop for help if they need it. Major System Functions Functional Features (What the system actually does) Record Orders Online: The cashier can type the customer's name, the weight of the clothes, and the price into the computer instead of writing in a paper book. Track Laundry Steps: The workers (Labandera) can click simple buttons to show what is happening to the clothes, like moving them from "Washing" to "Drying" to "Ready." Count Specific Clothes: The system can record the exact number and type of clothes for certain customers. This stops people from saying the shop lost their items. Track Payments: The system will save if an order is "Paid" or "Unpaid," which makes it very easy to handle "wash now, pay later" customers. Send Automatic Text Messages: The system will automatically send an SMS to the customer when their clothes are ready, if there is a power outage, or if they forgot to pick up their clothes. Calculate Daily Sales (Reports): The system will automatically add up all the money the shop made in a day or a month, so the owner does not have to do the math by hand. Customer Online Checker: Customers can use a simple web page on their phones to check if their laundry is finished. Non-Functional Features (How the system behaves and feels) Easy to Use (User-Friendly): The app will be very simple. Workers only need to learn a few clicks, and customers will have a very easy screen to look at. Safe and Secure: The information is protected. Customers can only see their own laundry, and only the Owner or Admin can look at the daily money and reports. Mobile-Friendly: The customer app and the delivery driver features will work smoothly and look good on small smartphone screens. Fast and Reliable: When a worker clicks a button to say the laundry is done, the system updates quickly so the customer gets the text message right away. Information/Data needed To make the new computer system work, it needs to collect and save specific everyday information. First, we need basic customer details, like their names and phone numbers, so the system can send them text messages. Second, we need laundry details for every single order. This includes the weight of the clothes, the exact number of clothing items (to stop customers from saying things are missing), and any special washing instructions. Third, we need money details, which means recording the total price and saving if the customer has already "paid" or if the order is still "unpaid." Finally, the system needs tracking details to remember exactly what step the clothes are in like washing, drying, or ready for pickup—and worker details to know which employee is doing the job. Expected System Outputs (What we will build) The final project will be delivered in two ways: a Web App (Website) and an Android App. Both the Lavhanan employees and the customers will be able to log in and use both of these platforms to check their laundry or do their work. System Constraints (Limitations) We cannot build an iOS (Apple/iPhone) version of the mobile app. This is because the specific programming tools (framework) we are using to build the project only support Android. However, this is not a big problem because iPhone users—whether they are employees or customers—can simply open the Web App on their phone's internet browser to use the system perfectly fine. Security Requirements To keep the business and customer information safe, the system will have strict security rules. First, everyone using the app must log in with a secure password so strangers cannot get inside. Second, the system will use strict access limits based on exactly who is logging in. Customers can only see their own laundry tickets and cannot look at other people's phone numbers. For the employees, normal workers can only see and update the laundry orders they are working on. The Manager is given a middle level of access; they can see all of the laundry orders and customer details to help solve shop problems, but they cannot change the most private system settings. Finally, only the Owner or Admin is allowed to see the big financial sales reports and the total money earned. The system will also protect the records by stopping anyone from accidentally deleting an order, especially if the customer still has an "unpaid" bill. Other Requirements/Constraints There are a few other important rules and limits for this project. First, the business owner actually owns the computer server and keeps it right at the laundry shop. Because the server is nearby, the workers can still use the system on the shop's local Wi-Fi even if the outside internet is slow or goes down. However, the shop will still need some internet connection to send the automatic text messages and to let customers check their laundry from their own homes. Second, the new computer system must be able to connect to a thermal receipt printer, so the shop can keep printing small paper tags for the laundry baskets. Third, the workers and the manager must use Android phones, Android tablets, or a normal computer, since there is no Apple iPhone version. Finally, the system must include a very simple video tutorial so everyone can easily learn how to use the new app. expected system output would be webapp or website and android app. the constraint is we can't develop ios version because the framework we will use is for android both can be used by employees and customers

item.title: Brief History of BPO in the Philippines
item.description: One of the most robust sectors in the Philippines right now is the information technology and business process outsourcing (IT-BPO) sector. More than just a lucrative enterprise, the IT-BPO sector has also proven to be the largest and fastest-growing industry in the country. There is no denying its major role in providing quality jobs and encouraging economic activity and investment even in areas outside Metro Manila.Of course, the IT-BPO industry was not an overnight affair. Credit is due to the handful of individuals who saw the potential in the business in its early stages. Among them are the likes of Rainier "Bong" Borja, who is often regarded as the most articulate voice of the Philippine BPO industry;Karen Batungbacal for her early involvement and series of contact center firms; andSecretary Mar Roxas, who, during his tenure as secretary of the Department of Trade and Industry, saw the potential of the industry, reached out to key leaders to promote foreign investment, and helped shape the landscape of BPO into what it is today. 1992 — First Contact Center: Frank Holz, under the Accenture group, created the first contact center in the Philippines. 1995 — Special Economic Zone Act: The Philippine Congress passed this act, lowering area requirements for development and offering tax incentives to attract foreign investors. 1997 — First BPO Multinational: Sykes Asia established operations, becoming the first multinational BPO company in the Philippines. 1999 — First Call Center: Jim Franke and Derek Holley founded eTelecare, which became widely recognized as the country's first call center. 2000 — GDP Contribution: The BPO industry accounted for 0.075% of the Philippines' total GDP. 2001 — Expansion & Job Creation: PeopleSupport, a US-based outsourcing center, restructured its business operations to move to the Philippines, generating approximately 8,400 jobs. 2003 — Convergys Expansion: Convergys Corp. opened two call centers in the country. Chosen alongside India by company president Jack Freker, this formed a key part of their global growth plan. 2005 — Global Market Share: The Philippines captured 3% of the global BPO market, which represented 2.4% of the country's GDP. 2006 — PLDT Ventus & Growth: PLDT Ventus emerged at the forefront of the local BPO landscape, helping boost the Philippine domestic economy by 5.4%. Around 11,000 individuals were employed across North America, Europe, and Asia. 2010 — BPO Capital Title: The Philippines earned the recognition of being the "world's BPO capital", employing over 525,000 people in call centers and generating $8.9 billion in revenue. 2011 — Top Job Provider: The sector became one of the fastest-growing job providers in the private sector, generating $11 billion in revenue, employing 638,000 Filipinos, and comprising 4.9% of total GDP. 2012 — Continued Expansion: Industry revenues reached 5.4% of total GDP, maintaining a growth rate of around 46% annually since 2006. 2013 — Milestone Numbers: Revenue climbed to $15.5 billion, with full-time employment reaching 900,000 Filipinos. 2016 — Long-Term Projection: Projections estimated the industry would generate 1.3 million new jobs with a 17% annual growth rate. 1992: Accenture establishes the first contact center in the Philippines. 1995: The Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) is established. 1999: eTelecare, the first call center company in the country, is founded. 2000: The BPO sector contributes 0.075% to the Philippine GDP. 2001: Establishment of the Contact Center Association of the Philippines (CCAP). 2002: Proposal to revise Republic Act 7916 to extend tax perks to PEZA-registered BPOs. 2005: The BPO industry captures 3% of the global market. 2006: The BPO sector experiences a 46% annual growth rate. 2008: The Philippines surpasses India in BPO growth. 2010: The Philippines officially earns the title of the BPO capital of the world. 2019: The BPO industry thrives despite pandemic-related shutdowns. 2020: According to PEZA, IT-BPO investment pledges increased by 37% from January to July 2020. 2021: The outsourcing industry continues to grow despite the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. 2022: IBPAP actively lobbies for the permanent adoption of hybrid work. 2023: The country boasts more than 700 BPO companies. 2024: More than 850 BPO companies. 2028: 59 billion target revenue. 2030: AI roadmap estimated a $92 billion GDP contribution by 2030. item.description:
title: "Case 1: It's Global Warming, Stupid - System Dynamics Analysis" tags: systems-thinking ibpap-case-study climate-change hurricane-sandy causal-loop-diagram date: 2026-08-17 type: case-analysis Based on the Case 1 text, a hurricane operates within an interconnected system of atmospheric, oceanic, and socio-economic variables. Fossil Fuel Burning & Carbon Emissions: The combustion of coal, petroleum, and fossil energy that traps heat in the atmosphere. Quantification: Natural gas emits ~50% less carbon than coal when burned for power; new fuel-efficiency standards aim to cut vehicle greenhouse emissions by 50% by 2025. Global Warming & Ocean Temperatures: Thermal energy absorbed by the oceans and atmosphere. Quantification: Recorded as global thermal spikes, such as July 2012 being the hottest month in the continental U.S. since record-keeping began in 1895. Atmospheric Moisture Retention: The volume of water vapor held by warmer air and drawn into storms. Quantification: Percentage increase in atmospheric humidity resulting in intense precipitation dumped during severe weather. Arctic Icemelt & Blocking High Patterns: Melting Arctic sea ice altering atmospheric jet streams and sending cold air southward to collide with warm ocean storms. Quantification: Extent of Arctic ice loss contributing to atmospheric pressure blocking patterns. Human Mortality & Displacement: Fatalities and forced evacuations resulting from storm surges and urban flooding. Quantification: At least 40 U.S. deaths and hundreds of thousands of evacuated residents during Hurricane Sandy. Economic Losses & Structural Damage: Total financial destruction, grounded commercial transportation, and power utility failure. Quantification: $50 billion in expected losses from Hurricane Sandy; $1.06 trillion in total weather disaster losses in North America from 1980 through 2011; 8 million homes without power; >15,000 flights grounded. Weather-Related Loss Event Frequency: The rate of catastrophic weather events over time. Quantification: A nearly quintupled (5x) increase in weather-related loss events in North America over three decades. Political Will for Climate Action & Infrastructure Spending: Public and governmental urgency to fund disaster response (FEMA), waterproof transit, or regulate carbon emissions. Quantification: Percentage of public belief in global warming (67% in October 2012, down 10 points from 2006) and renewable energy generation share (<15% of U.S. electricity). Placing high value on immediate economic growth and consumer gratification drives increased burning of fossil fuels (coal and oil) to power factories, offices, and transport. Higher carbon emissions trap atmospheric heat, causing global atmospheric and ocean temperatures to rise. Warmer oceans provide more energy to storms, while a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, increasing hurricane strength and precipitation. Stronger hurricanes cause massive economic destruction, power grid shutdowns, and infrastructure flooding. Severe economic strain causes politicians and the public to focus heavily on short-term economic recovery, encouraging promises to mine more coal and drill more oil rather than invest in long-term climate action.
Increased storm energy leads to catastrophic economic damage, flooding cities and destroying power systems. High-profile disasters like Hurricane Sandy force climate change back onto the political agenda, building political support for disaster preparedness, renewable energy transitions, and carbon taxation. Regulatory measures (such as power plant emission caps, fuel-efficiency rules, and cap-and-trade systems) reduce overall fossil fuel burning. Lowering carbon emissions slows the rate of heat trapped in the atmosphere and ocean upper layers. Reduced ocean and atmospheric warming limits the thermal energy available to fuel supercharged tropical cyclones.

item.title: Pax Silica Variables
item.description:
Executive Summary Pax Silica is a U.S.-led economic security initiative designed to build resilient, allied supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductor manufacturing, and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure outside of Chinese influence. For the Philippines, this initiative centers around strategic industrial projects like the Luzon Economic Corridor (connecting Subic, Clark, Manila, and Batangas) and major proposed infrastructure in New Clark City. Resource Intensity: Microchip fabrication and AI data centers require immense volumes of high-purity cooling water and continuous high-voltage electricity. Position in Global Value Chain: Moving from raw mineral extraction (nickel, copper) to domestic processing, testing, and advanced fabrication. Geopolitical Alignment: Deepening defense and industrial ties with the U.S., Japan, and Australia vs. preserving trade relations with China (the country's largest trade partner). Socio-Environmental Balance: Mitigating environmental degradation, chemical waste, and indigenous land displacement while attracting high-value foreign direct investment (FDI). Opportunities & Gains Surge in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Unlocks significant capital from the U.S., Japan, and partner nations to develop infrastructure along the Luzon Economic Corridor. Value-Chain Upgrading Shifts the economy from exporting low-margin raw minerals toward high-value domestic refining, component assembly, and chip testing. High-Skilled Job Creation & Mitigation of Brain Drain Establishes career pathways for local engineers, technicians, and data scientists, encouraging technical talent to remain in the Philippines. Domestic Critical Mineral Processing Captures downstream value by processing domestic nickel, cobalt, and copper deposits locally rather than exporting raw ore. Infrastructure Modernization Accelerates development of regional deepwater ports, modern freight logistics, high-voltage power grids, and fiber-optic backbones. Technology and Knowledge Transfer Stimulates technical capability sharing and R&D partnerships between global tech conglomerates, local industries, and Philippine universities. Integration into Allied Tech Supply Chains Solidifies the Philippines as a trusted node within secure global supply networks alongside the U.S., Japan, South Korea, and Australia. Leveraging Special Economic Zone Frameworks
Capitalizes on fiscal incentives under the CREATE MORE Act (RA 12066) to attract major foreign technology locators and support services. Accelerated Renewable Energy Grid Expansion Catalyzes large-scale investments in clean energy generation and grid resilience to meet the strict power demands of tech hubs. Enhanced Geopolitical & Trade Leverage Elevates the Philippines' strategic role in international diplomacy, providing stronger negotiation leverage in global trade agreements. Vulnerabilities & Risks Severe Water Resource Depletion Chip fabrication and AI cooling demand tens of millions of liters of fresh water daily (projected up to 130M liters/day), threatening agricultural and residential supplies during severe droughts like El Niño. Power Grid Instability & Price Hikes Gigawatt-scale energy consumption by data centers and foundries puts immense pressure on grid capacity, risking higher electricity costs for consumers. Hazardous Chemical & Toxic Waste Risks Semiconductor manufacturing uses heavy metals, fluorides, and solvents. Inadequate treatment could contaminate vital Central Luzon groundwater systems. Agricultural & Ancestral Land Displacement
Large-scale land conversion in Central Luzon risks displacing agrarian communities and indigenous Aeta Ancestral Lands. Increased Target Risk in Geopolitical Conflicts Hosting critical U.S.-aligned technology nodes makes Philippine facilities strategic points of concern during regional tensions in the Indo-Pacific. Intellectual Property Asymmetry High-value intellectual property, proprietary software, and primary profits remain concentrated in foreign multinationals, leaving local operations in lower-margin support roles. Risk of "Enclave Economy" Isolation Tax incentives and tax-free economic zones may lead to isolated corporate hubs that generate limited direct tax revenues for municipal governments. Strained Local Municipal Infrastructure Rapid influxes of industrial facilities can overwhelm local roads, sanitation, housing, and public health systems before tax revenues scale up. Trade Friction with Primary Partners Deep alignment with a U.S. initiative explicitly intended to bypass China risks triggering trade friction or economic retaliation from Beijing. Low Job Yield Per Resource Unit Advanced fabricators and AI data centers are highly automated, creating relatively few direct long-term operational jobs relative to their massive footprint in land, power, and water. Owen N. Estrera SYS100 - A
Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity -> High-Skilled Jobs & Local R&D Building and expanding high-tech facilities creates direct demand for local engineers, data scientists, and technicians, keeping top talent from moving abroad. High-Skilled Jobs & Local R&D -> Supply Chain Competitiveness A skilled local workforce and active research drive innovation, making the country's tech sector faster, smarter, and more reliable on the global stage. Supply Chain Competitiveness -> Foreign Direct Investment & Capital A strong, reliable tech sector builds international confidence, encouraging foreign companies and allied nations to invest more capital into the Philippines. Foreign Direct Investment & Capital -> Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity That incoming investment funds larger facilities, advanced equipment, and better infrastructure, expanding overall industrial capacity and restarting the loop at a bigger scale.
Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity -> Water & Power Demand Surges Running chip factories and cooling large AI data centers requires immense amounts of continuous electricity and fresh water, causing regional energy and water demands to surge. Water & Power Demand Surges -> Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks Heavy resource consumption drains local groundwater tables and strains the power grid, leading to water shortages, higher utility bills for local residents, and risks of toxic chemical waste. Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks -> Semiconductor & AI Industrial Capacity If left unchecked, severe water shortages, power outages, and public opposition naturally slow down or halt further industrial expansion, acting as a brake on growth. Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks -> PH Sustainable Policies (Activating Solutions - B2) Rising environmental strain forces government intervention and policy enforcement—activating mandates for water recycling (Zero Liquid Discharge), renewable energy programs (GEOP), and indigenous community protections (IPRA). PH Sustainable Policies -> Resource Scarcity & Environmental Risks Enforcing these sustainable practices reduces raw water usage, shifts energy demands to renewables, and resolves community disputes, directly relieving resource scarcity.

The student is the primary end user who starts core self-service functions, including submitting advising requests, viewing advisor free time, making appointments, rescheduling or cancelling existing appointments and also viewing or downloading advising notes. item.title: Role-Based Simulation and Analysis
item.description: Form groups of 3 - 4 students. Each group will assume the roles involved in a systems integration project: Note: Each member of the group will be assigned any of this responsibilities. Project Manager IT Systems Lead Business Unit Manager End-user Representative Each group selects or is assigned a fictional project, such as: University Student System Hospital Management System Laboratory Information System Small retail POS + Inventory System + E-commerce System As a group, simulate a planning session. Discuss and document: Each role’s responsibilities and concerns Potential organizational issues, such as: Resistance to new technology Poor communication between departments Conflicting priorities Lack of user training Budget/timeline constraints Propose solutions or best practices to address these challenges in paragraph format. Discuss in paragraph what were the main managerial/organizational issues discussed during the group discussion. How did your group resolve role conflicts or challenges? What are the real-world implications of these issues in actual IT projects? What best practices would you recommend for IT managers leading integration projects? Project Managertraffic allocated money student staffResolution of Role Conflicts and Challenges Proposed Solutions and Best Practices for Organizational Challenges Real-World Implications of Organizational Issues in Actual IT Projects Recommended Best Practices for IT Managers Leading Integration ProjectsThe Project will be a University Student SystemProject Name: University Student System Integration Project My Role: Project Manager Responsibilities: Oversee the entire integration project from initiation to closure. Manage the allocated money, ensure timelines align with the academic calendar, and act as the bridge between technical teams, administration, and end-users. Concerns: Staying within strict budget constraints, scope creep, ensuring all departments are aligned, and preventing timeline delays that could disrupt the upcoming semester. Responsibilities: Design the technical architecture, handle data migration from legacy systems, ensure system security, and guarantee the infrastructure can handle high traffic (e.g., thousands of students accessing the system simultaneously during enrollment). Concerns: Technical debt from old legacy systems, server crashes during peak traffic, data breaches, and integrating disjointed databases (e.g., financial and academic records). Responsibilities: Ensure the new system correctly enforces university policies, handles financial transactions accurately, and provides necessary reporting tools for the staff. Concerns: Disruption to daily administrative operations during the transition, data corruption during migration, and the possibility that the allocated money won't cover essential operational features. Responsibilities: Advocate for the needs of students and teaching staff. Test the system for usability, accessibility, and intuitive design. Concerns: A steep learning curve, confusing interfaces, system downtime during critical periods (like submitting grades or paying tuition), and lack of proper onboarding. Resistance to new technology: Many university staff members and veteran professors may be accustomed to the legacy system or paper-based processes. They may view the new system as an unnecessary complication rather than an upgrade. we can use a a paper based protocol. in the paper based protocol, what the veteran staff will do is they get the necessary printed papers, fill those up and scan it with an interpreter software so that the physical document is read and turned into digital automatically. they can also edit the document if there are some things the interpreter could not read but if they still wouldn't get it, there will be another staff that will help them with the protocol if they need help with it. Poor communication between departments: The IT department might use technical jargon that the Business Unit Managers (Registrar/Finance) do not understand. Conversely, IT might not fully grasp the intricate academic rules and prerequisites needed for the system. We can have a policy dealing with that. First for the poor communication with the Professionals. in the policy we will state that when talking to an employee with the same profession they can talk technically but when dealing with employees with different a profession, they have to talk in english rather than technically to avoid jargon. Conversely, for IT not getting the full grasp of academic rules and prerequisites. we will ask the university registrar the academic rules, the prerequisites, the student handbook and other things the system may need. Conflicting priorities: The IT Lead may want to delay the launch to ensure perfect system stability and handle high traffic seamlessly, whereas the Project Manager and Business Unit Manager are pressured to launch the system immediately before the next enrollment period begins. Since the university has an academic calendar, there are no excuses to delay the launch of the system before enrollment however, what we can do is to launch the system with a limit to its traffic, let the student be advised to refresh the page if it doesn't load and let the IT lead start a branch of the System so that they can address the high traffic issue. after fixing the high traffic issue, we can update the system quetly when there is little traffic like midnight Lack of user training: With thousands of students and hundreds of staff members, providing adequate training is a massive logistical challenge. Without it, users will struggle, leading to a flood of support tickets and frustration. Different groups need different levels of training staff who use the system daily need hands-on sessions, while students and faculty just need simple guides for the features they'll actually use. Skipping this step means people get confused, support teams get overwhelmed, and users may avoid the new system together, even if it works fine technically. That's why training should be planned and budgeted early, not added in at the last minute. Budget/timeline constraints: The project is bound by a fixed allocated money pool and a rigid academic calendar. Any delays or requirements for additional funds will require difficult trade-offs, such as cutting planned features (like a mobile app version) to launch on time. To handle these constraints without failing the project, we will adopt a phased rollout strategy based on a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) approach. We will allocate the budget to prioritize core functionalities needed for the immediate academic calendar—such as enrollment processing, student records, and basic finance—and push non-essential features, like the mobile app version, to a Phase 2 release. During our group discussion, we found some critical managerial and organizational issues in regards to integrating a University Student System. first obstacle was the resistance to new technology among veteran staff members, they rely on legacy paper-based processes which doesn't really fit in the innovation of a new system. we also analyzed the poor comunnication between departments, mostly on the technical jargons that will arise when employees of different professions talk to each other and conversely, how IT lacks familiarity of the academic handbook rules and enrollment prerequisites. Moreover, we also encountered conflicting priorities between the IT Lead-who prioritized stability and high traffic controll but then the business administration faced pressure to launch the system before the academic deadline. lastly, we addressed the massive challenge of training thousands of students and staff members within the our allocated money and rigid calendar constraints To solve these challenges, our group made practical, structured solutions for each issue. To minimize technology resistance, we designed a traditional paper-based protocol where where veteran staff complete printed forms that are audomatically digitalized using an OCR/interpreter software, supported by staff who will assist them whenever reading errors happen. To break down department communication barriers, we made a strict communication policy: Professionals must clear, non-technical english when coordinating across departments, and IT must directly reference the registrar's handbook for rule validation. now for user training. we made a tiered approach providing intensive hand on sessions for staff who will interact with the system daily while giving the students and faculty a quick-start guide to the system they will interact with. Finally, to manage financial and timeline constraints, we used a Minimum Viable Product or MVP strategy, focusing on core enrollment and record features while moving non-essential features like a mobile app to a future update or future phase.As a Project Manager, resolving problems between the IT Systems Lead and the Business Unit Manager regarding lunch readiness needed a collaborative approach. when we had our discussion session, we acknowledged that because the university operates on a fixed academic calendar, a delay or a launch beyond the enrollment was not an option. We found alternatives such as user queueing system but we realized it would cause unnecessary friction to the traffic. Drawing directly from our recent lessons on the Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), all of us agreed to launch the working core system on the schedule time while handling initial high traffic by setting soft connection caps or limits and advising the students to refresh the webpage if there's some issues. at the same time the IT team developed a parallel branch to resolve server load issues and pushing small incremental updates during low-traffic hours (like midnight) so that students and staff will not notice the transition of the update and there will be no interruptions. The Organizational and techical issues discussed have real world consequences if left unmanaged. some major platforms like facebook and discord show that even a massive infrastructure can crash when hit with unexpected traffic spikes. in an academic setting, a total enrollmet crash will stall the registration and disrupts tuition collection and will also trigger a lot of public frustration. Miscommunications and overlooked technical security can also lead to catasrophic data breaches, just like the registrar API leaks seen in our university (https://sms.norsu.top). Furthermore, failing to consider for user training or budgetary limits often result to widepsread user rejection, abandoned software investments and severe administrative backlogs that will threaten the university's operational continuity.For IT managers leading complex systems integration project, theres some best practices things i recommend Enforce Plain-Language Communication: Make sure to have a clear cross-departmental communication to negate technical jargon and ensure technical requirements meet perfectly with operational and academic policies Adopt and Agile and Phased Deployment Strategy: Focus on initial releases on an MVP to satisfy strict calendar deadlines, using continuous, incremantal updates during low traffic hours to improve system performance without causing downtime Implement Strict Change Control and Prioritization: protect allocated money and timeline by prioritizing core functions needed by primary stakeholders before considering extra enhancements. Prioritize Early Security and Traffic Testing: start rigorous load testing and API security audits early on in the development life cycle to prevent high traffic crashes and data culnerabilities before a public launch

item.title: The Identity Prism
item.description: Differentiate between biological sex, gender, and sexual orientation. Understand the social, cultural, and psychological implications of these differences. Reflect on personal identity and the importance of fostering an inclusive, diverse environment. Human experience is shaped by three interconnected yet distinct dimensions: Sex: The biological aspects of maleness or femaleness (chromosomes, anatomy, hormones). Gender: The social interpretation of sex (masculinity, femininity, cultural expectations). Sexuality: The totality of an individual's personal experience regarding their sex and gender. Biological sex is the biological dimension determined by reproductive anatomy and genetic markers. It is typically assigned at birth based on external physical characteristics. Components of Sex Biology: Chromosomes: Genetic structures (XX typically denotes female; XY typically denotes male). Hormones: Chemical drivers (females generally have higher levels of estrogen/progesterone; males have higher testosterone). Anatomy: Internal reproductive organs and external genitalia. The Intersex Spectrum: Biological sex is not strictly binary. Intersex refers to individuals born with chromosomal variations or composite genital characteristics combining male and female traits. Occurs in approximately 1 in 1,500 births (APA, 2006). Replaces the historical term hermaphroditism. Gender is a social construct. Because humans are "meaning-making organisms," higher-order thinking leads societies to assign cultural meaning to biological sex. The Socialization Timeline: Birth: Immediate assignment of gendered expectations (e.g., blue for boyhood, pink for girlhood). Childhood: Family members select toys, clothes, and activities based on interpreted sex. Adolescence: Rules expand into strict social and behavioral expectations. Adulthood: Norms influence career paths, fields of study, and societal roles. Heteronormativity: The assumption or societal standard that judges behavior as "normal" only when it strictly conforms to traditional expectations associated with biological sex (e.g., expecting girls to be gentle/caring and boys to be strong/assertive). Evolving Social Norms: Gender expression standards change over time. For example, 60 years ago, women wearing pants faced heavy social disapproval, whereas today it is standard fashion. Rejection of traditional gender roles (e.g., boys rejecting rough sports or girls rejecting dresses) represents natural variations in human expression. Gender identity is an internal, deeply felt sense of who one is—experiencing oneself as a man, a woman, non-binary, or another identity. Cisgender: Individual whose internal gender identity aligns with the biological sex assigned to them at birth. Transgender: Individual whose internal gender identity does not align with the biological sex assigned to them at birth. Transgender Woman: Assigned male at birth; identifies as a woman. Transgender Man: Assigned female at birth; identifies as a man. Note on Medical Transition: Some transgender individuals choose gender reassignment processes to align physical traits with identity, while others do not due to personal beliefs, cultural context, or economic factors. Sexual orientation describes the pattern of emotional, romantic, and sexual attraction toward others. Developmental Timeline: Emotional and sexual attraction typically begins developing around ages 6 to 8 (Psychological Association of the Philippines - PAP). Dating and relationship experimentation generally occurs during adolescence. Key Definitions: Heterosexual (Straight): Attraction to individuals of the opposite sex/gender. Homosexual (Gay/Lesbian): Attraction to individuals of the same sex/gender. Bisexual: Attraction to individuals of both male and female sexes/genders. LGBT: An acronym representing the Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender community. Human identity is not a simple binary switch. Instead, it operates on four independent, continuously variable axes: Key Takeaway: Every human being represents a unique, custom configuration across these four independent sliders. Personal Discovery: Sexual orientation and gender identity are deeply personal internal processes. A person's identity can only truly be known if they choose to share their lived experiences and feelings. Impact of Prejudice: Individuals subjected to discrimination, stigma, or prejudice suffer negative psychological effects. Goal: Creating safe, inclusive, and empathetic environments enables everyone to express their authentic selves without fear of harm or social isolation. What term describes biological markers such as XX/XY chromosomes? Answer: Biological Sex. How frequently do intersex traits occur in births? Answer: Roughly 1 in 1,500 births (APA, 2006). What term describes someone whose internal gender identity differs from their assigned sex at birth? Answer: Transgender. At what age range does attraction typically begin developing according to the PAP? Answer: Ages 6 to 8.

item.description: game dev focusA system is a group of interacting, interrelated, or interdependent components that form a complex and unified whole. Physical Components: Tangible items like machinery, body organs, or physical parts. Intangible Components: Non-physical elements like processes, relationships, company policies, information flows, and internal states of mind (feelings, values, beliefs). Embedded Networks: Systems exist as nodes inside larger networks. For example, an R&D department is a system within a company, which is a system within an industry, which is a system within an economy. To determine whether something is a functional system or merely a collection, it must exhibit these five properties:A system’s parts must all be present for it to carry out its purpose optimally. Collection: Removing a cashew from a bowl of mixed nuts leaves fewer nuts, but does not alter the essential nature of the bowl. System: Redefining jobs or removing team members in an R&D department directly alters the system’s performance and relationships. Key Rule: Dividing a system destroys its function ("If you divide an elephant in half, you don't get two smaller elephants"). Parts must be organized in a specific structure. In a fruit bowl (collection), swapping the position of apples and oranges changes nothing. In a company (system), randomly swapping accounting specialists with assembly line workers disrupts the entire organization. Every system serves a discrete purpose in relation to the broader system in which it is embedded. This purpose gives the system its individual integrity.Systems maintain stability through continuous internal adjustments and feedback loops. Body temperature fluctuates around 98.6°F based on exertion and sweat response. A company’s profit margins fluctuate weekly as bills are paid and invoices collected, maintaining an average baseline over time. Feedback is the transmission and return of information that triggers a change in behavior. Immediate Feedback: Steering a car into a turn gives instant visual cues to adjust the wheel. Delayed Feedback: Decisions like employee layoffs may yield immediate financial cost-cutting, but delayed negative feedback (burned-out staff, low morale, high turnover, reduced quality) takes months or years to manifest. Systemic understanding is divided into three distinct levels. The deeper down the pyramid you go, the higher your leverage for long-term change. /\ / \ [ Events ] -> React /----\ / \ [ Patterns ] -> Adapt /--------\ / \ [ Structure ] -> Create Change /------------\ What it is: A single snapshot moment in time (e.g., a building catches fire, a project misses a deadline). Action Mode: React! Limitation: Solving problems at this level yields only short-lived fixes and does not stop recurrence. What it is: Trends or recurring changes in events over time (e.g., sales declining over 3 years, high engineer turnover over 6 months). Action Mode: Adapt! Benefit: Allows you to anticipate trends and plan responses based on historical behavior. What it is: The invisible web of interrelationships and causal connections driving the patterns. Action Mode: Create Change! Benefit: Offers high-leverage, self-sustaining solutions (e.g., implementing building fire codes and sprinkler policies instead of just putting out fires). Why Diagram Systems? Because all systems are part of larger open networks, no diagram can capture 100% of a system. However, creating Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs) allows individuals and groups to externalize mental models, surface hidden assumptions, and identify leverage points for systemic changes. When probing structure, look for circular feedback chains rather than linear cause-and-effect: Budget Cuts lead to Administrative Staff Layoffs. Fewer admins increase remaining Engineers' Workloads. High workloads damage Morale. Low morale leads to Engineers Leaving. Staff loss increases Workloads even further for those left behind, reinforcing the downward spiral.

item.title: game dev focus
item.description: In game design, a system isn't just a block of code—it’s how gameplay elements interact to create player flow. Collection: Stacking 10 random assets in a folder. Moving one out doesn't break the game. System: Your combat scene in Godot. If you remove the Hitbox detection, the whole combat system stops working. When your game breaks or feels unfun, you can analyze it at three levels: /\ / \ [ EVENT ] -> "My game hit 15 FPS just now." (React) /----\ / \ [ PATTERN ] -> "FPS drops whenever 10+ enemies spawn." (Adapt) /--------\ / \ [ STRUCTURE ] -> "Enemy spawning logic lacks Object Pooling." (Fix Architecture) /------------\ Event Level (React): You reboot the engine or kill the process. Short-term fix. Pattern Level (Adapt): You notice lag spikes happen specifically during heavy wave spawns. Structure Level (Create Change): You fix the underlying node lifecycle (e.g., reusing enemy nodes instead of calling .instantiate() every frame). This permanently fixes the lag. Systems maintain balance or scale up through feedback loops: Reinforcing Loop (Snowball Effect): Balancing Loop (Homeostasis): ⚡ ADHD Focus Guardrail Watch out for Feature Creep! When building systems in Godot, ship the core loop first (Movement Attack Damage). Do not start adding inventory crafting, skill trees, or 20 weapon types until that single core loop feels smooth!

item.title: Note taking assignment
item.description: deadline: jul 23, 12:00PM 2026On your notebook, write the appropriate meaning and roles of the following terminologies in Philippine BPO: GCC PSIA GDAP CCAP HIMAP GICC ACPI IBPAP IT-BMP SLA NDA SMP BPS TAT HR VA OM TSR SEO CSR with your name and class section hand written perpendicularly along the side of the page. Take photo of such notes then post/save the same on or before 12 noon july 23 This cluster of acronyms heavily represents the IT & Business Process Management (IT-BPM) sector, global shared services, and standard business operations. IBPAP – IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines The primary umbrella association and trade organization for the IT-BPM sector in the Philippines, working with government and academia to drive industry growth. PSIA – Philippine Software Industry Association An industry association representing software development, tech solutions, and IT service companies. GDAP – Game Developers Association of the Philippines The organization representing local game design, interactive media, and digital entertainment studios. CCAP – Contact Center Association of the Philippines The trade association representing contact centers, call centers, and customer experience operations. HIMAP – Healthcare Information Management Association of the Philippines An association representing companies providing health IT, medical coding, transcription, and healthcare BPO services. GICC – Global In-House Center Council The industry association representing captive corporate shared service centers and global capability centers.akoa ACPI – Animation Council of the Philippines, Inc. The trade group representing animation studios, 2D/3D visual artists, and post-production service providers. GCC – Global Capability Center (Primary IT-BPM Context) An in-house, offshore/nearshore facility established by a global company to perform core operations, engineering, IT, or analytics tasks internally. (Alternative Macroeconomic Context: Gulf Cooperation Council) IT-BMP / IT-BPM – Information Technology and Business Process Management The overarching business sector that delivers technology services, back-office operations, and customer support via outsourcing or shared services. (Also referred to as IT-BMP for IT-Business Management Program/Process). BPS – Business Process Services Outsourced operational tasks and functions (e.g., HR, accounting, customer care) managed by an external provider or internal shared service team. SMP – Service Management Program (IT-BPM Context) An industry-designed academic track integrated into university curricula to prepare students for management and operational roles in the IT-BPM sector. (Alternative Marketing Context: Social Media Platform / Social Media Plan) SLA – Service Level Agreement A formal contract defining specific service performance standards (e.g., response time, resolution rate, system uptime) between a service provider and client. NDA – Non-Disclosure Agreement A legal contract designed to protect confidential business details, client data, and proprietary trade secrets from unauthorized disclosure. TAT – Turnaround Time The total elapsed time required to process, complete, and deliver a task or request from start to finish. HR – Human Resources The business unit handling recruitment, payroll, employee management, training, and corporate policy. VA – Virtual Assistant A remote administrative or specialist contractor providing virtual support to a business or individual. (Also refers to Voice Analytics in contact center tech). OM – Operations Manager A managerial role overseeing daily team workflows, delivery quality, efficiency, and operational execution. TSR – Technical Support Representative A frontline customer service specialist trained to troubleshoot technical, network, hardware, or software issues. CSR – Customer Service Representative / Corporate Social Responsibility Operations Role: Customer Service Representative – A agent handling customer inquiries, orders, and issue resolution. Corporate Governance: Corporate Social Responsibility – Business practices intended to make a positive impact on society and the environment. SEO – Search Engine Optimization Digital marketing techniques aimed at improving website content visibility and ranking on search engine result pages. files: https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/1wMf-X987BxQc10EKSYGFQxWHzOndkrbs
